claims.text: Catalytic performance is governed by dynamic modulation of the transition metal oxidation state under reaction conditions.
Electrochemical potential cycling can promote a particular metal oxidation state.
Potential-cycled catalysts will exhibit higher activity than catalysts held at a static potential.
Potential-cycled catalysts will exhibit better selectivity than catalysts held at a static potential.
The catalysts begin with active sites in a mixed-valence state.
Potential cycling preferentially shifts the surface oxidation-state distribution.
The cycling-induced oxidation state facilitates more effective adsorption of reaction intermediates.
The cycling-induced oxidation state facilitates activation of reaction intermediates.
More effective intermediate adsorption and activation enhance catalytic turnover.
Static-potential operation preserves the catalyst's initial oxidation-state distribution.
The initial oxidation-state distribution is less favorable for electron transfer.
Potential cycling will produce a measurable increase in turnover frequency relative to static-potential operation.
Potential cycling will improve target-product selectivity relative to static-potential operation.
The performance improvement will coincide with a shift in oxidation-state distribution toward an active form.
The proposed relationship applies under moderate oxidative and reducing conditions typical of ambient-temperature aqueous electrochemistry.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to Cu, Fe, and Ni catalysts in similar catalytic systems.
The magnitude of performance improvement may vary with the metal and reaction system.
The optimal oxidation state may vary with the metal and reaction system.
